1.headline: Japan and India Will Train Together
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Will Japanese soldiers fire missiles in India? Yes, they will.
Japan and India had a big meeting in Tokyo. Their defense ministers came. Their foreign ministers came too. Four leaders sat at one table.
They made a plan. Japanese soldiers will train in India. They will use real missiles. The two armies will practice together.
Japan also wants to give India a special antenna. It helps ships talk to each other. Both sides want to move fast on this.
This is new for Japan. For many years, Japan did not sell weapons. Now it is changing its rules.
Again, Japan and India will work closer on defense. Their soldiers will train together.
Thank you for listening.

일본 군인들이 인도에서 미사일을 쏠까요? 네, 그렇습니다.
일본과 인도가 도쿄에서 큰 회의를 열었습니다. 두 나라의 국방장관이 왔습니다. 외교장관들도 왔습니다. 네 명의 장관이 한 테이블에 앉았습니다.
그들은 계획을 세웠습니다. 일본 군인들이 인도에서 훈련합니다. 실제 미사일을 사용합니다. 두 나라 군대가 함께 연습합니다.
일본은 또 인도에 특별한 안테나를 주고 싶어 합니다. 이 안테나는 배들이 서로 연락하도록 돕습니다. 두 나라는 이 일을 빨리 진행하고 싶어 합니다.
이것은 일본에게 새로운 일입니다. 오랫동안 일본은 무기를 팔지 않았습니다. 이제 일본은 규칙을 바꾸고 있습니다.
다시 말해, 일본과 인도는 국방에서 더 가깝게 협력합니다. 두 나라 군인들이 함께 훈련합니다.
들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

2.headline: Japan and India Agree to Train Together With Real Missiles
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Japanese soldiers will soon fire real missiles in India. Why is this happening?

On Thursday, Japan and India held an important meeting in Tokyo. The defense ministers and foreign ministers of both countries were there. People call this kind of meeting a two-plus-two. It was their fourth meeting like this.

According to news reports, the two countries agreed to work more closely on defense. Japanese troops will do live-fire missile training in India. Live-fire means they will use real weapons, not fake ones. This will happen during joint drills, when both armies practice together.
They also agreed to speed up talks about a Japanese antenna called UNICORN. It is advanced technology that helps navy ships communicate. Japan hopes to send it to India.
This is a big change for Japan. After World War Two, Japan made strict rules to keep peace. For a long time, it did not sell deadly weapons. But Japan has relaxed these rules in recent years.
Japan and India are both large countries in Asia. Their leaders say they want a free and open region.
To sum up, Japan and India are building stronger defense ties, with joint missile training and shared technology.
Thank you for listening.
tr: 좋은 아침입니다. 영어 아침 뉴스입니다.
일본 군인들이 곧 인도에서 실제 미사일을 쏘게 됩니다. 왜 이런 일이 일어날까요?
목요일, 일본과 인도가 도쿄에서 중요한 회의를 열었습니다. 두 나라의 국방장관과 외교장관이 참석했습니다. 사람들은 이런 회의를 '2+2'라고 부릅니다. 두 나라가 이런 회의를 연 것은 네 번째입니다.
보도에 따르면, 두 나라는 국방 분야에서 더 긴밀히 협력하기로 합의했습니다. 일본 군대는 인도에서 실사격 미사일 훈련을 합니다. 실사격이란 가짜가 아닌 진짜 무기를 쓴다는 뜻입니다. 이 훈련은 두 나라 군대가 함께 연습하는 합동 훈련 중에 이뤄집니다.
두 나라는 또 '유니콘'이라는 일본 안테나에 관한 협상을 서두르기로 합의했습니다. 해군 함정끼리 통신하도록 돕는 첨단 기술입니다. 일본은 이것을 인도에 보내기를 바랍니다.
이것은 일본에게 큰 변화입니다. 제2차 세계대전 이후, 일본은 평화를 지키기 위해 엄격한 규칙을 만들었습니다. 오랫동안 일본은 살상 무기를 팔지 않았습니다. 하지만 최근 몇 년 동안 일본은 이 규칙을 완화해 왔습니다.
일본과 인도는 둘 다 아시아의 큰 나라입니다. 두 나라 지도자들은 자유롭고 열린 지역을 원한다고 말합니다.
정리하면, 일본과 인도는 합동 미사일 훈련과 기술 공유로 더 강한 국방 관계를 만들고 있습니다.
들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

3.headline: Japan and India Agree on Live-Fire Missile Training and Faster Tech Sharing
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Why would Japanese troops fire missiles in India? It is part of a new defense plan between two of Asia's biggest democracies.

According to news reports, the defense and foreign ministers of Japan and India met in Tokyo on Thursday. This kind of meeting is called a two-plus-two, because two ministers from each country sit down together. It was the fourth meeting of this kind. India sent Defense Minister Rajnath Singh and Foreign Minister Jaishankar. Japan was represented by Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.

The two sides agreed to make their military partnership stronger. Japanese troops will hold live-fire missile training at firing ranges in India during joint drills. Live-fire training means soldiers use real weapons, not practice ones. The countries also agreed to speed up talks on a Japanese communications antenna for navy ships, called UNICORN. Japan wants to transfer this advanced technology to India.

This is a big shift for Japan. After World War Two, Japan followed strict pacifist principles, which means rules against using military force. For decades, it did not sell weapons abroad. But Japan has relaxed these rules a lot. It has even lifted its ban on exporting lethal weapons, which are weapons that can kill.

Why does this matter? Japan and India are large economies in the Indo-Pacific region. Their leaders often say they want the region to stay free and open, with clear rules for everyone. Stronger defense ties between them could shape security across Asia.
To sum up, Japan and India agreed to train together with real missiles and to move faster on sharing military technology.
Thank you for listening.

4.headline: Japan, India Deepen Defense Ties With Live-Fire Drills and Antenna Talks
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.
Japanese troops firing live missiles on Indian soil would have been hard to imagine not long ago, but that is exactly what Tokyo and New Delhi have now agreed to.

According to news reports, the defense and foreign ministers of Japan and India met in Tokyo on Thursday for the fourth round of their so-called two-plus-two dialogue. India was represented by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh and External Affairs Minister Jaishankar, while Japan sent Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.

Under the agreement, Japanese forces will conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges during joint exercises. The ministers also pledged to strengthen their security partnership and to accelerate negotiations on transferring an advanced Japanese naval communications antenna, known as UNICORN, to India. The system combines several antennas into a single mast on warships.

The deal reflects how far Japan has moved from its postwar pacifist stance. For decades, the country kept tight limits on its military and on arms exports. In recent years, however, it has significantly relaxed those principles and lifted its ban on exporting lethal weapons, as part of a broader security and economic strategy.

For India, closer ties with Japan offer access to high-end technology and a reliable partner in the Indo-Pacific. Both governments regularly stress their shared goal of a free, open and rules-based region, and defense industry cooperation is now becoming a central part of that relationship.
The UNICORN project in particular has been under discussion for some time, so the pledge to accelerate it suggests both sides want faster, more visible results.
To sum up, Japan and India have agreed to hold live-fire missile drills together and to speed up talks on sharing naval technology, marking another step in their growing military partnership.
Thank you for listening.

5.headline: Tokyo and New Delhi Step Up Military Ties With Live-Fire Drills and Tech Transfer Talks
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.
Not so long ago, the idea of Japanese troops test-firing missiles on Indian ranges would have been unthinkable; on Thursday, it became official policy.

According to news reports, the defense and foreign ministers of Japan and India convened in Tokyo for the fourth iteration of their two-plus-two dialogue, a format that brings both countries' diplomats and defense chiefs to the same table. New Delhi was represented by Defense Minister Rajnath Singh and External Affairs Minister Jaishankar, while Tokyo fielded Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.

The headline outcome was an agreement allowing Japanese forces to carry out live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges during joint exercises. The ministers also vowed to deepen their security partnership and to fast-track negotiations on transferring UNICORN, a sophisticated Japanese naval antenna system that consolidates multiple communications antennas into a single mast, to India.

Taken together, the moves underscore just how far Japan has drifted from the strict pacifism that defined its postwar identity. For decades, the country hemmed in its armed forces and all but ruled out arms sales abroad. Over the past several years, however, Tokyo has substantially loosened those constraints, culminating in the lifting of its ban on exporting lethal weapons, as part of a wider overhaul of its security and economic strategy.

For India, the partnership holds out the prospect of cutting-edge technology and a dependable ally in a region where both capitals routinely champion a free, open and rules-based order. Defense industrial cooperation, long the missing piece in an otherwise flourishing relationship, now appears to be moving to the forefront.

Whether the momentum translates into concrete deals remains to be seen; arms transfers are notoriously slow, and negotiations over UNICORN have been under way for some time. Still, the symbolism of Japanese missiles being fired on Indian soil is hard to overstate.

To sum up, Japan and India have agreed to stage live-fire missile drills together and to expedite talks on a key naval technology transfer, a sign that their defense relationship is entering a new and more ambitious phase.
Thank you for listening.

들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

1.headline: Voyager 1 Is One Light-Day Away
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Can you send a message that takes one full day? Now you can, to Voyager 1.
Voyager 1 is a small spaceship. It has no people inside. It left Earth in 1977.
This week, it reached a new place. It is now one light-day from Earth. Light is very fast. But light from Earth takes one day to get there.
That is about sixteen billion miles away. No other machine from Earth is so far.
Voyager 1 is very old. It is almost fifty years old. But it still sends messages home.
Did you know? Voyager 1 carries a gold record. It has sounds and pictures from Earth.
Again, Voyager 1 is now one light-day from home.
Thank you for listening.
tr: 좋은 아침입니다. 영어 아침 뉴스입니다.
꼬박 하루가 걸리는 메시지를 보낼 수 있을까요? 이제 보이저 1호에게는 그렇습니다.
보이저 1호는 작은 우주선입니다. 안에 사람은 없습니다. 1977년에 지구를 떠났습니다.
이번 주, 보이저 1호가 새로운 곳에 도착했습니다. 이제 지구에서 1광일 떨어져 있습니다. 빛은 아주 빠릅니다. 하지만 지구에서 출발한 빛이 거기까지 가는 데 하루가 걸립니다.
약 160억 마일 떨어진 거리입니다. 지구에서 만든 기계 중 이렇게 멀리 간 것은 없습니다.

다시 말해, 보이저 1호는 이제 지구에서 1광일 떨어져 있습니다.

2.headline: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Imagine sending a text message and waiting a whole day for it to arrive. That is now true for NASA and Voyager 1.
Voyager 1 is a space probe, a robot spaceship with no people on board. It left Earth in 1977. This week, it became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth.
What is a light-day? It is how far light travels in twenty-four hours. That is about sixteen billion miles, or twenty-six billion kilometers.
This means a radio signal from Earth needs a full day to reach the probe. According to NASA, sending a command and getting an answer now takes about two days.
Voyager 1 was first made to fly past Jupiter and Saturn. But it kept going. In 2012, it left our solar system's bubble and entered interstellar space, the space between the stars.
The probe is old, and NASA has turned off some parts to save power. But it still talks to Earth.
Did you know? Voyager 1 carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of life on Earth.
To sum up, Voyager 1 is now one light-day away, farther than anything humans have ever built.
Thank you for listening.

3.headline: Voyager 1 Becomes the First Human-Made Object One Light-Day From Earth
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
How far away is one day? For NASA's Voyager 1, the answer is about sixteen billion miles.

According to news reports, Voyager 1 reached a historic milestone early on Wednesday. A milestone is an important point in a long journey. The space probe is now one light-day from Earth, which means light needs a full twenty-four hours to travel between them. That is about sixteen billion miles, or twenty-six billion kilometers. No human-made object has ever gone this far.

Voyager 1 left Earth in September 1977. It was first designed to fly past Jupiter and Saturn and send back pictures. But after that, it simply kept going, at about thirty-eight thousand miles an hour. In 2012, it crossed into interstellar space, the area between the stars, outside the bubble around our sun.

The distance makes daily work tricky for the team. NASA's project scientist Linda Spilker explained that a command now takes a whole day to arrive. So it takes about two days to find out whether the probe followed the order.

The spacecraft is also getting old. To save power, NASA has switched off several of its science instruments. Still, some are working, and the probe keeps sending data home. NASA even invited fans to celebrate by flashing the letters V, G and R in Morse code.
Did you know? Voyager 1 carries a golden record, a kind of time capsule with sounds and images from Earth.
To sum up, Voyager 1 is now one light-day away, the farthest point any human-made object has ever reached.
Thank you for listening.

4.headline: Voyager 1 Crosses the One Light-Day Mark in Interstellar Space
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.
Nearly half a century after it left Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 has set yet another record: it is now so far away that its signals take a full day to reach us.

According to news reports, the probe crossed the one light-day mark early on Wednesday, Pacific time. A light-day is the distance light covers in twenty-four hours, roughly sixteen billion miles, or twenty-six billion kilometers. Voyager 1 is the first human-made object ever to get that far.

Launched in September 1977, the spacecraft was originally built for a close look at Jupiter and Saturn. Once that mission was complete, it simply kept traveling outward at around thirty-eight thousand miles per hour. In 2012, it became the first probe to enter interstellar space, leaving behind the protective bubble created by the sun.

The milestone highlights the practical challenges of talking to a machine so remote. Project scientist Linda Spilker noted that a command sent from Earth now needs twenty-four hours to arrive, meaning the team waits about two days to learn whether an instruction was carried out.

Age is another concern. Engineers have gradually shut down several science instruments to conserve the probe's shrinking power supply, though at least a few remain active and continue to send back data. To mark the occasion, NASA encouraged the public to flash the letters V, G and R in Morse code.
Its twin, Voyager 2, is traveling more slowly and is expected to reach the same distance around 2035.
Did you know? Both Voyagers carry a gold-plated record of sounds and images, a message in a bottle for anyone who might find it.
To sum up, Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth, a distance no other human-made object has ever reached.
Thank you for listening.

5.headline: Voyager 1 Drifts Past the One Light-Day Threshold, a First for Humanity
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.
Somewhere in the cold, dark expanse beyond our solar system, a spacecraft launched when disco was still in fashion has just quietly rewritten the record books.

According to news reports, NASA's Voyager 1 slipped past the one light-day threshold early on Wednesday, Pacific time. In other words, a beam of light, or a radio signal, now needs a full twenty-four hours to bridge the gap between the probe and Earth, a span of roughly sixteen billion miles, or twenty-six billion kilometers. No object built by human hands has ever ventured so far.

Voyager 1 lifted off in September 1977 with a comparatively modest brief: to swing past Jupiter and Saturn and beam back close-up images. Having fulfilled that mission, it carried on hurtling outward at some thirty-eight thousand miles an hour, and in 2012 it became the first probe to breach interstellar space, slipping beyond the sun's protective bubble.

The achievement throws the logistical headaches of deep-space communication into sharp relief. As project scientist Linda Spilker pointed out, any command now takes a day to arrive, so engineers must wait roughly two days to confirm that the spacecraft has done as it was told.

Time is also taking its toll. Mission controllers have progressively powered down a number of science instruments to eke out the probe's dwindling energy supply, although a handful remain operational and continue to relay data. In a playful nod to the moment, NASA invited the public to flash the letters V, G and R in Morse code.
Its sibling, Voyager 2, is on a slower trajectory and is not expected to hit the same mark until around 2035.
Did you know? Each Voyager carries a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth, a cosmic message in a bottle for whoever, or whatever, might one day stumble across it.
To sum up, Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, a fitting milestone for one of the most enduring missions in the history of space exploration.
Thank you for listening.

1.headline: What Is a Multicultural Family in Korea?
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Can a family of Korean citizens be multicultural? In Korea, yes.
Korea has a law for multicultural families. Many of these families have one parent from another country. Some parents later become Korean citizens. Their family can still be multicultural.
These families can get help. Their children can get into day care faster. They can also get help with school and housing.
There are more of these families now. In 2025, there were about four hundred fifty thousand. Ten years ago, there were fewer than three hundred thousand.
One mother came from China eighteen years ago. She says her life feels almost the same as a Korean life.
Again, a multicultural family in Korea can be a family of Korean citizens.
Thank you for listening.
tr: 좋은 아침입니다. 영어 아침 뉴스입니다.
한국 국민으로만 이뤄진 가족도 다문화 가정일 수 있을까요? 한국에서는 그렇습니다.
한국에는 다문화 가족을 위한 법이 있습니다. 이런 가족 중 다수는 부모 한 명이 다른 나라 출신입니다. 어떤 부모는 나중에 한국 국민이 됩니다. 그래도 그 가족은 여전히 다문화 가정일 수 있습니다.

2.headline: What Korea Means by a Multicultural Family
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
In Korea, a family can be called multicultural even when everyone in it is a Korean citizen. How does that work?

According to the Korea Herald, Korea has a special law for multicultural families. It started in 2008. It covers families where a person from another country marries a Korean. It also covers some families where a parent became a Korean citizen later.
This label is useful. It can help children get a place in day care sooner. It can also bring support for education and housing.

The number of these households is growing. In 2025, the census counted about four hundred fifty thousand multicultural households. A census is an official count of the people in a country. Ten years earlier, there were fewer than three hundred thousand.

There is good news, too. More children from these families now go to college. But some people still face unfair treatment. About thirteen percent of marriage immigrants and new citizens said they had felt it.
One woman from China has lived in Korea for eighteen years. She says her daily life is not very different from a Korean's.
To sum up, Korea's idea of a multicultural family is wider than many people think.
Thank you for listening.
tr: 좋은 아침입니다. 영어 아침 뉴스입니다.
한국에서는 가족 모두가 한국 국민이어도 다문화 가정이라고 불릴 수 있습니다. 어떻게 그럴까요?
코리아헤럴드에 따르면, 한국에는 다문화 가족을 위한 특별한 법이 있습니다. 이 법은 2008년에 시작되었습니다. 다른 나라 사람이 한국인과 결혼한 가족이 대상입니다. 부모 한 명이 나중에 한국 국민이 된 일부 가족도 포함됩니다.
이 이름표는 쓸모가 있습니다. 아이들이 어린이집에 더 빨리 들어가는 데 도움이 될 수 있습니다. 교육과 주거 지원도 받을 수 있습니다.
이런 가구 수는 늘고 있습니다. 2025년 인구주택총조사에서는 약 45만 다문화 가구가 집계되었습니다. 인구주택총조사란 한 나라의 사람 수를 세는 공식 조사입니다. 10년 전에는 30만 가구가 안 되었습니다.
좋은 소식도 있습니다. 이제 이런 가정의 아이들이 더 많이 대학에 갑니다. 하지만 일부는 여전히 부당한 대우를 받습니다. 결혼이민자와 귀화자 약 13퍼센트가 차별을 느낀 적이 있다고 답했습니다.
중국 출신의 한 여성은 한국에서 18년 동안 살았습니다. 그녀는 자신의 일상이 한국 사람의 일상과 크게 다르지 않다고 말합니다.
정리하면, 한국의 다문화 가정 개념은 많은 사람이 생각하는 것보다 넓습니다.
들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

3.headline: Who Counts as 'Multicultural' in Korea? More People Than You Might Think
p: Good morning. This is your morning news in English.
Here is a surprising fact: in Korea, a family can be officially multicultural even if every member is a Korean citizen.

According to a report by the Korea Herald, this comes from the Multicultural Families Support Act, a law passed in 2008. It mainly covers families formed when a marriage immigrant, a person who moves to Korea through marriage, weds a Korean citizen. But it also includes some families where a parent became a citizen later, through naturalization. Naturalization means officially becoming a citizen of a new country.
Being labeled multicultural can bring real benefits. Children may get priority on waiting lists for day care. Families may also receive help with education or housing.

These households are becoming more common. The 2025 census, an official count of the population, found about four hundred fifty-one thousand multicultural households. A decade earlier, the number was just under three hundred thousand. They now make up about two percent of all households.

There are signs of progress. The share of multicultural children going on to higher education rose from about forty-one percent in 2021 to nearly sixty-two percent in 2024. Still, thirteen percent of marriage immigrants and naturalized citizens said they had faced discrimination.

The families themselves often describe ordinary lives. One woman who moved from China eighteen years ago said daily life feels much like being Korean. Another mother said, with a smile, that she and her Korean husband argue about which country to cheer for at sports events.
To sum up, Korea's legal idea of a multicultural family is broad, and these families are a growing part of society.
Thank you for listening.
tr: 좋은 아침입니다. 영어 아침 뉴스입니다.
놀라운 사실 하나: 한국에서는 가족 구성원 모두가 한국 국민이어도 공식적으로 다문화 가정일 수 있습니다.
코리아헤럴드 보도에 따르면, 이것은 2008년에 만들어진 법인 '다문화가족지원법'에서 비롯됩니다. 이 법은 주로 결혼이민자, 즉 결혼을 통해 한국에 온 사람이 한국 국민과 결혼해 이룬 가족을 대상으로 합니다. 하지만 부모 한 명이 나중에 귀화로 국민이 된 일부 가족도 포함합니다. 귀화란 공식적으로 새 나라의 국민이 되는 것을 뜻합니다.
다문화로 분류되면 실질적인 혜택이 있을 수 있습니다. 아이들은 어린이집 대기 명단에서 우선권을 받을 수 있습니다. 가족은 교육이나 주거 지원도 받을 수 있습니다.
이런 가구는 점점 흔해지고 있습니다. 인구의 공식 집계인 2025년 인구주택총조사에서 다문화 가구는 약 45만 1천 가구로 나타났습니다. 10년 전에는 30만 가구에 조금 못 미쳤습니다. 이제 전체 가구의 약 2퍼센트를 차지합니다.
발전의 신호도 있습니다. 대학에 진학하는 다문화 가정 자녀의 비율은 2021년 약 41퍼센트에서 2024년 거의 62퍼센트로 올랐습니다. 그래도 결혼이민자와 귀화자의 13퍼센트는 차별을 겪은 적이 있다고 답했습니다.
가족들 스스로는 평범한 삶을 이야기하는 경우가 많습니다. 18년 전 중국에서 온 한 여성은 일상이 한국 사람으로 사는 것과 거의 같다고 말했습니다. 또 다른 어머니는 한국인 남편과 스포츠 경기에서 어느 나라를 응원할지를 두고 다툰다고 웃으며 말했습니다.
정리하면, 한국 법에서 말하는 다문화 가정의 개념은 넓으며, 이 가정들은 사회에서 점점 커지는 부분입니다.
들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

4.headline: Korea's Broad Definition of 'Multicultural' Shapes Who Gets Support
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.
In South Korea, a household made up entirely of Korean citizens can still be classified as multicultural, a fact that surprises many people, including some Koreans.

According to a report by the Korea Herald, the definition comes from the Multicultural Families Support Act, enacted in 2008. The law primarily covers families formed by a marriage immigrant and a Korean national, but it also extends to certain families in which every member already holds citizenship, for example when one parent was naturalized and the children became citizens at birth.

The classification carries practical weight. It can move children up day care waiting lists and open the door to assistance with education and housing, although some education subsidies are subject to an income cap. A number of universities also run separate admissions tracks for these students.

The population in question is growing steadily. The 2025 census counted roughly four hundred fifty-one thousand multicultural households, up from just under three hundred thousand a decade earlier, or about two percent of all households in the country.

Government survey data point to real progress. The share of multicultural children enrolled in higher education climbed from around forty-one percent in 2021 to almost sixty-two percent in 2024, narrowing the gap with the national rate by more than half. Even so, thirteen percent of marriage immigrants and naturalized citizens reported experiencing discrimination.

How far support should go is a matter of debate. President Lee Jae Myung said in October that policies should prevent discrimination without disadvantaging other families, while advocates argue that eligibility should be widened to include migrants outside the current family categories.
To sum up, Korea's legal definition of multicultural is broader than many assume, and it plays a growing role in deciding who receives public support.
Thank you for listening.

정부 조사 자료는 실질적인 발전을 보여 줍니다. 다문화 가정 자녀의 고등교육 취학률은 2021년 약 41퍼센트에서 2024년 거의 62퍼센트로 올라, 전국 평균과의 격차를 절반 넘게 줄였습니다. 그런데도 결혼이민자와 귀화자의 13퍼센트는 차별을 경험했다고 답했습니다.

정리하면, 한국 법의 다문화 정의는 많은 사람이 생각하는 것보다 넓으며, 누가 공공 지원을 받는지를 정하는 데 점점 더 큰 역할을 합니다.
들어 주셔서 감사합니다.

5.headline: Beyond Borders and Passports: How Korea Defines a 'Multicultural' Family
p: Good morning, and welcome to your morning news in English.

In South Korea, a family can hold nothing but Korean passports and still be officially deemed multicultural, a quirk of the law that says a great deal about how the country is grappling with its changing face.

According to a report by the Korea Herald, the label stems from the Multicultural Families Support Act, enacted in 2008. The legislation is aimed chiefly at households formed through the union of a marriage immigrant and a Korean national, yet its reach extends to families in which everyone is already a citizen, for instance where one parent was naturalized and the children acquired citizenship at birth.

Far from being a mere technicality, the designation can tip the scales in everyday life. It can bump children up day care waiting lists and unlock help with schooling and housing, though certain education subsidies are means-tested. Some universities even set aside dedicated admissions tracks for such students.

The constituency is expanding. The 2025 census tallied roughly four hundred fifty-one thousand multicultural households, up from just shy of three hundred thousand a decade earlier, accounting for around two percent of the national total.

On paper, integration appears to be gathering pace. Higher-education enrollment among multicultural children jumped from about forty-one percent in 2021 to nearly sixty-two percent in 2024, more than halving the gap with the national rate. Yet thirteen percent of marriage immigrants and naturalized citizens said they had encountered discrimination, a reminder that statistics only tell part of the story.

Behind the numbers, many of the families describe lives that are, in most respects, unremarkable. One woman who moved from China eighteen years ago told the paper that her day-to-day existence is not much different from being Korean.

Where to draw the line on support remains contentious. President Lee Jae Myung cautioned in October that assistance should guard against discrimination without tipping into unfairness toward other families, while advocates contend that eligibility ought to be broadened to migrants who fall outside existing family categories.
To sum up, Korea's expansive legal definition of a multicultural family reflects a society in transition, and the debate over who qualifies for help is far from settled.
Thank you for listening.
